title: I Hear There Are People Possessed by Madness
intro: Ibn Ashur brings together scattered quotations in praise of Umar ibn al-Ala and explains how he ordered them. Bashshar first answers people who profess not to recognise him, claiming both his Persian ancestry and his ties to Banu Amir. A lover’s go-between gives way to a patron whom the needy can approach and the caliph can trust with a war. The last comparison exposes a different sort of giver, whose promises gleam like a mirage.

translation: I hear there are people possessed by madness
who ask, “Who is that?” I was the landmark.
1.sharh: He treats the question about his identity as feigned ignorance or outright madness. A landmark is precisely the thing everyone else uses to find their bearings.

translation: Listen, you who take such pains to ask about me
so you may know me. I am the nose of nobility.
2.sharh: The nose is the part of the face that stands forward. Its Arabic name also calls up proud refusal to submit to humiliation, so the answer lays claim to both distinction and spirit.

translation: My branches grew among generous Banu Amir.
My roots are the Quraysh of the Persians.
3.sharh: The branches belong to his upbringing among an Arab tribe, the roots to his Iranian ancestry. Quraysh supplies an Arab listener with a comparison for his family’s standing.

translation: I can take a young man’s place
and win a girl till she cannot hold out.
4.sharh: He can perform a man’s part and, he claims, win a young woman’s affections. The Arabic names for the young man and woman form an audible pair.

translation: Many a girl was made one of a kind,
all other women seeming servants beside her.
5.sharh: The women have simply come into her presence, yet her distinction rearranges the whole company into a mistress and her attendants.

translation: An idol round which girls circle. When they visit,
they go round a wide-eyed beauty like a statue.
6.sharh: The visitors’ movements supply the comparison as much as the woman’s looks. She holds the still centre while a circle forms around her.

translation: They keep stroking her sides
as the Stone is touched in greeting.
7.sharh: The circling is followed by touch. The comparison draws on the pilgrim’s greeting of the Black Stone and conveys the visitors’ almost devotional attention.

translation: And a fair woman, youth’s bright moisture laughs
in her face for you when she smiles.
8.sharh: The freshness of youth has acquired its own smile. The expression for that freshness runs across the Arabic line break like the animation moving over her face.

translation: I thirsted for her. She gave me nothing to quench it,
nor healed me of my sickness.
9.sharh: The woman has the two things he says he needs, water and a cure. Refusing both sets up the unexpectedly brisk advice she gives him next.

translation: She said, “You fell in love. Then go and die well,
as Urwa died, grief heaped on grief.”
10.sharh: Her polite-sounding farewell sends him to join a famous dead lover. Urwa’s story gives her a precedent for dismissing a perfectly live suitor.

translation: When I saw that love was killing me,
and I was neither neighbour nor cousin,
11.sharh: His predicament has a practical side. No accepted tie gives him a reason to enter her household, so the sentence waits for a third person to act.

translation: I secretly sent Abu Mijlaz to her.
What a man when he finds his opening and acts.
12.sharh: The celebrated conqueror in love now needs an intermediary. He praises the friend for judging the moment and having the resolve to use it.

translation: He kept at it till she yielded to him.
He came back and what was forbidden us was allowed.
13.sharh: The poem leaves the negotiation offstage. Its success is measured by the change in what the woman will permit when the intermediary comes back.

translation: Safra, a young man is no rock.
He is a target set up for sorrow and care.
14.sharh: He asks Safra to recognise ordinary human vulnerability. The griefs are like archers whose target, unlike a stone, can feel every hit.

translation: I tell her, when my wealth runs low,
my aims are thwarted and the livestock gone,
15.sharh: The change of subject is gradual. He still addresses a woman, but loss of livestock gives him a new reason to set out on the road.

translation: “When I grow poor, I keep the night journey alive
to Ibn al-Ala, physician for want.”
16.sharh: He knows where poverty can be treated. The new physician answers the earlier lover’s plea for a cure with something a patron can actually give.

translation: Umar’s generosity called me to him,
and my people’s saying, “He is a vast sea.”
17.sharh: No formal invitation was needed. The community’s report that Umar gives on an oceanic scale has done the work of summoning the poet.

translation: But for what they said, I would never
praise a fragrant sprig before smelling it.
18.sharh: A sensible judge tests the fragrance for himself. By taking other people’s word for this particular sprig, the poet both compliments Umar and explains his own advance praise.

translation: You seeker who would reach
the stars with an easy, modest effort,
19.sharh: The disproportion is between the height of the destination and the size of the effort. The rival’s journey will measure how hard it is to reach Umar’s standard.

translation: you heard of Ibn al-Ala’s high distinction
and set out after it. You are nowhere near it.
20.sharh: Hearing of an achievement and matching it are very different distances to travel. The abrupt “you are not there” leaves the aspirant well short of the destination.

translation: When a wish for amusement crosses his heart,
he takes his pleasure in giving and striking warriors.
21.sharh: The verb for taking his pleasure repeats the sound of the noun for amusement. Umar’s diversions are the two demanding public roles his admirers expect him to fill.

translation: He relishes giving gifts and shedding blood,
and goes out bearing blessings or reprisals.
22.sharh: Only one consonant changes between blessings and reprisals. The sound brings close together the very different prospects of Umar’s friends and enemies.

translation: Tell the caliph, if you reach him,
as a sincere adviser. A suspect one is no good.
23.sharh: The poet casts his praise as practical advice for the ruler. Whether the listener can trust the messenger matters when the message recommends a commander.

translation: “If enemy wars have woken you,
wake Umar to take them on. Then sleep.”
24.sharh: Waking and sleeping distribute responsibility with extraordinary economy. The ruler can relinquish the very vigilance that his commander takes up.

translation: A man who never sleeps on a debt of blood
and drinks no water except with blood.
25.sharh: Rest and the most basic drink are both made conditional on vengeance. The harsh image extends the promise that Umar can stay awake on the caliph’s behalf.

translation: Whenever he campaigns, his birds foretell
a victory, and he foretells gifts for us.
26.sharh: The birds are read as omens for the expedition. He repeats the verb for bringing good news and turns the victory into something his own listeners can hope to share.

translation: Once he speaks, he stands by his word.
A no or a yes puts an end to trouble.
27.sharh: Even his refusal counts in his favour. Either answer has the value of ending the petitioner’s uncertainty on the spot.

translation: Some men stand close in what they promise,
and in what they do lie under a grave mound.
28.sharh: A man can sound close enough to touch and be as unreachable in action as the dead. This is the opposite of a ruler whose two possible answers both mean something.

translation: Like water running in a mirage, you see it gleam
and find none of it where you stand.
29.sharh: Moving water describes what a thirsty eye thinks it sees. When the traveller tries to obtain the promised thing, it has exactly as much substance as that gleam.

1.2.5.meaning: A conspicuous landmark, often a mountain.

2.2.3-4.head: أَنف الكَرَم
2.2.3-4.meaning: “The nose of nobility”, its foremost part, with an echo of pride.

3.1.4-5.head: بَنو عامِر
3.1.4-5.meaning: Banu Amir ibn Sa'sa'a, the Arab tribe to which Bashshar was affiliated as a client.

3.2.3-4.head: قُرَيش العَجَم
3.2.3-4.meaning: “The Quraysh of the Persians”, a claim to comparable rank among his own ancestors.

4.1.2.head: أَغنى
4.1.2.meaning: To suffice or fill another person’s place.

4.2.1.head: أَصبى
4.2.1.meaning: To entice someone into falling in love.

6.1.1.head: دُوار
6.1.1.meaning: Duwar, an idol around which people went in procession.

6.2.2.head: حَوراء
6.2.2.meaning: A woman with strikingly contrasting dark pupils and white eyes.

7.2.3-4.head: الحَجَر المُستَلَم
7.2.3-4.meaning: The Black Stone in Mecca, touched or kissed during circumambulation.

8.1.3-4.head: ماء الشَّباب
8.1.3-4.meaning: “The water of youth”, youthful freshness. The word for youth ends in the next half.

10.2.3.head: عُروَة
10.2.3.meaning: Urwa ibn Hizam, Afra’s lover, remembered for dying of love.

12.1.3-4.head: أَبو مِجلَز
12.1.3-4.meaning: Abu Mijlaz, the intermediary in the love episode. Ibn Ashur gives no established personal name.

13.1.4.head: أَنابَ
13.1.4.meaning: Relented and gave an affirmative answer.

14.1.1.head: صَفراء
14.1.1.meaning: Safra, the woman addressed. An initial particle calls to her.

14.2.2.head: نُصب
14.2.2.meaning: A target set up to be shot at.

15.2.4.meaning: Livestock, especially camels as a form of wealth.

16.2.2-3.head: اِبن العَلاء
16.2.2-3.meaning: Ibn al-Ala, Umar, an Abbasid commander and governor of Tabaristan who served al-Mansur and al-Mahdi.

17.2.4.head: خِضَمّ
17.2.4.meaning: Vast and full of water, said of a sea of generosity.

20.2.4.head: ثَمَّ
20.2.4.meaning: There, at the level the rival hopes to reach.

21.2.4.meaning: Warriors formidable enough to be hard to face.

23.2.1.head: نَصوح
23.2.1.meaning: Acting as a wholly sincere adviser.

26.1.5.head: طَير
26.1.5.meaning: Birds interpreted as favourable omens at the start of a journey.

28.2.4.meaning: A grave or the heap of stones marking one.

29.1.2.head: السَّراب
29.1.2.meaning: A mirage, the apparent sheet of water above hot ground.

29.2.3.meaning: Where you are. Ibn Ashur prints two separate words, finds the text obscure and conjectures “when you reach it”.
